skill.name: enact-hello-go
skill.description: Runs a minimal Go program that greets a supplied name and prints the Go runtime version.
skill.summary: Run a simple Enact Go greeting example.
skill.author: EnactProtocol

security_audit.summary: Both static detections are false positives in context. The Go import block is normal Go syntax, and the flagged shell text is a documentation code fence showing how to run the example.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 3 starts a normal Go import block for fmt, os, and runtime, not a JavaScript dynamic import() expression. The program only reads an argument and prints local greeting text and runtime information.
Lines 32-34 are a fenced bash usage example for running the skill, not Ruby backtick execution. No prompt-injection text or hidden shell-substitution directive appears in that documentation block.

content.value_statement: Developers need a small working Enact skill to verify local setup and learn the package format. This skill runs a Go greeting command with a name input and shows a simple structured tool pattern.
actual_capabilities: Accepts a name value as input.
Prints a personalized greeting from a Go program.
Prints the Go runtime version used during execution.
Defines simple input and output schemas in SKILL.md.
Runs through an Enact command using a Go container image.
limitations: It is a demonstration skill, not a general Go project generator.
It only accepts a single name string.
It does not validate names beyond the declared string input type.
It does not perform network calls, file management, or build automation.

use_cases.title: Verify Enact Setup
use_cases.description: Run a small Go skill to confirm that Enact can execute a local example.

use_cases.title: Learn Skill Structure
use_cases.description: Review a compact SKILL.md and Go file to understand basic input, output, and command fields.

use_cases.title: Test Tool Integration
use_cases.description: Use a predictable greeting response when checking Claude, Codex, or Claude Code workflows.

prompt_templates.title: Run the Default Greeting
prompt_templates.prompt: Use enact-hello-go with the default name and show me the greeting.

prompt_templates.title: Greet a Specific Person
prompt_templates.prompt: Run enact-hello-go with the name Alice and summarize the result.

prompt_templates.title: Explain the Skill Layout
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how enact-hello-go connects its input schema, command, and Go source file.

prompt_templates.title: Adapt the Example
prompt_templates.prompt: Use enact-hello-go as a reference and describe how to extend it with one additional string input.

output_examples.output: The skill returns a friendly greeting for Alice and reports the Go version used.
The skill uses World as the default name and prints the runtime version.

best_practices: Use simple names when testing the command input.
Review SKILL.md before adapting the example for another language.
Keep demo changes small so output remains easy to verify.
anti_patterns: Do not use this example as a production command runner.
Do not pass secrets or private data as the greeting name.
Do not expect it to compile or manage larger Go modules.

faq.question: What does this skill do?
faq.answer: It runs a small Go program that prints a greeting and the Go runtime version.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it make network requests?
faq.answer: No. The reviewed files show local command execution only.

faq.question: Can I change the greeting name?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill defines a name input with World as the default.

faq.question: Is this a complete Go development assistant?
faq.answer: No. It is a compact example for learning and testing Enact skill execution.

faq.question: Why does it print the Go version?
faq.answer: The Go program prints the runtime version so users can see which Go environment ran the example.
